faq.a: Reaching orbit needs an enormous change in speed, and a rocket must carry its own oxygen as well as fuel. So about nine tenths of a rocket's mass at launch is propellant.
asks: How much of a rocket is fuel?

faq.q: What happens when a rocket stage separates?
faq.a: The used stage's engines shut down, bolts or pushers release it, and it drifts away. Then the next stage's engine ignites, a moment called staging.

faq.q: How fast does a rocket go to reach orbit?
faq.a: Low Earth orbit needs a sideways speed of about 7.8 kilometres per second, roughly 28,000 kilometres per hour. Going that fast sideways keeps a satellite falling around Earth instead of back down.

faq.q: Why not just build one huge rocket stage?
faq.a: A single stage would carry its heavy empty tanks all the way up, wasting fuel. With today's materials, a single stage to orbit would leave almost no room for the satellite.
asks: Why can't a rocket reach orbit in one stage?

faq.q: What happens to the dropped stages?
faq.a: Most fall into the ocean or burn up in the atmosphere. Some, like the first stage of SpaceX's Falcon 9, fly back and land so they can be used again.

facts: The Saturn V rocket that took astronauts to the Moon had three stages.
Low Earth orbit needs a speed of about 7.8 kilometres per second.
